name: Aphelion Goliath
specific_features: Massive ring system of captured asteroidal debris
description: Aphelion Goliath orbits at the outer reaches of its star system, spending most of its long year in the cold darkness far from stellar warmth. Its upper atmosphere is among the coldest measured on any gas giant, with ammonia ice forming thick polar caps that extend nearly to the equator. Deep thermal upwelling zones punch through these frozen layers periodically, creating brief windows of relative warmth that close within hours. A massive ring system, composed of captured asteroidal debris, encircles the planet in a broad band that casts complex shadows across the cloud tops.

The toxic atmosphere is dominated by hydrogen and helium with significant ammonia and methane fractions, the cold temperatures keeping these compounds in complex phase states that shift between gas, liquid, and solid. The ring system creates a visual spectacle when backlit by the distant star, the ice and rock fragments forming a glittering halo that extends for thousands of kilometers. The planet's moons navigate this debris field in cleared orbital paths, their gravity sweeping channels through the ring.

Aphelion Goliath's ring system appears to be relatively young on geological timescales, likely formed from the tidal disruption of a large moon or captured body within the last hundred million years. The ring composition is heterogeneous, containing both rocky and icy fragments of different origins, suggesting multiple capture or disruption events. Some fragments contain organic compounds of unexpected complexity, possibly from a body that once harbored life.

The planet's extreme distance from its star makes it an expensive target for resource extraction, though its helium-3 reserves are substantial. The ring system offers more accessible mining opportunities, with the asteroidal fragments containing diverse mineral compositions that can be harvested with conventional equipment. A ring-mining station has been proposed, which would also serve as a staging point for deep-space expeditions beyond the system's outer boundary.
